1.d4 d5 2.c4.name: Queen's Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.c4.background: One of the oldest known openings: it is mentioned in the Göttingen manuscript of 1490 and was analysed by Gioachino Greco in the 17th century. It did not become common until the 1873 Vienna tournament, and it was played in all but two of the 34 games of the 1927 World Championship match between Capablanca and Alekhine.
1.d4 d5 2.c4.strategy: Attacks d5 from the wing and offers a pawn that Black cannot keep without conceding something, since White can win it back or gain time. White aims for the bigger centre and lasting pressure on d5; Black usually holds d5 and accepts a cramped game, which it frees with the pawn breaks ...c5 and ...e5.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Zukertort Variation
1.d4 d5 2.Nf3.background: 2.Nf3 is the second most common move after 1.d4 d5, behind the Queen's Gambit 2.c4, and the position is also frequently reached via 1.Nf3.
1.d4 d5 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops the kingside knight to a square from which it covers e5 and d4, without deciding the pawn structure. White keeps every main set-up open and chooses the system once Black has shown a plan, trading the immediate pressure of c4 for flexibility. A quiet, flexible start that often leads into other structures.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4.name: London System
1.d4 d5 2.Bf4.background: Named after the 1922 London tournament, where the opening was played seven times, including in games by Capablanca, Alekhine and Rubinstein. James Mason was the first master-level player to use it regularly, at Vienna 1882, London 1883 and New York 1889.
1.d4 d5 2.Bf4.strategy: Develops the c1 bishop outside the pawn chain before e3 can lock it in, and plans a compact set-up that needs little theory. The set-up makes few demands on Black, who can develop freely, so White gets a low-risk, solid game with little early pressure.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Chigorin Variation
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight, puts pressure on d5 and prepares e4, but takes c3 from the c-pawn, so the usual c4 break is not available and d4 loses its natural support. White trades the lasting pressure of the Queen's Gambit for freer piece play.

1.d4 d5 2.Bg5.name: Hodgson Attack
1.d4 d5 2.Bg5.background: Named after the English grandmaster Julian Hodgson, who studied it extensively and found several new ideas; Preston Ware had already tested it in the 1880s. It was a very rare line until the 1980s, when players including Michael Adams and Tony Miles tried it. It is also called the Levitsky Attack, after Stepan Levitsky, and the Pseudo-Trompowsky.
1.d4 d5 2.Bg5.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain, where it attacks e7 and stands ready to answer ...Nf6 with Bxf6, doubling Black's f-pawns. The cost is that b2 is left undefended and the bishop can be harassed by ...h6, so Black gets a solid game with easy development.

1.d4 d5 2.e3.strategy: Supports d4 and opens the f1 bishop, heading for a compact set-up with a solid pawn centre. The c1 bishop is shut in behind the pawn, while Black can develop ...Bf5 outside the chain at once. Sound and low-risk, but passive, because nothing is done against d5.
1.d4 d5 2.e3.name: Queen's Pawn Game

1.d4 d5 2.e4.strategy: Offers the e-pawn for quick development, hoping to follow up with Nc3 and f3. Theory gives Black several ways to equalise, so the gambit is almost never seen at top level; Black can also simply decline it.

1.d4 d5 2.g3.strategy: Prepares Bg2, which pressures d5 along the long diagonal, in a fianchetto set-up that can add queenside pressure later. Sound but slow: d5 is not challenged yet, so Black can develop without difficulty.

1.d4 d5 2.b3.strategy: Prepares Bb2, which backs up d4 from behind, though the d4-pawn blocks the bishop's view along the long diagonal. Sound but slow: nothing is done against d5, so Black completes development at ease.

1.d4 d5 2.f4.strategy: Takes e5 and aims for a compact set-up with a firm pawn wall in the centre. It is playable, but it leaves e4 as a hole for a black knight, opens the e1–h4 diagonal, and makes the c1 bishop a bad bishop behind its own pawns. Black develops easily.
1.d4 d5 2.f4.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Mason Attack

1.d4 d5 2.c3.strategy: Supports d4 and opens the d1–a4 diagonal, so an early ...Bf5 can be met by Qb3 against the b7-pawn. The cost is that the b1 knight loses c3 and a later c4 takes a second tempo; Black develops freely.

1.d4 d5 2.a3.strategy: A rook-pawn move that neither develops a piece nor challenges d5. White's only gain is control of b4, while Black develops freely.

1.d4 d5 2.a4.strategy: Gains a little queenside space but weakens b4, and it neither develops a piece nor challenges d5. Black develops at ease.

1.d4 d5 2.b4.strategy: Gains queenside space but leaves the b4-pawn loose: after ...e6 the f8 bishop attacks it, and ...Bxb4 would come with check, so White must spend a tempo on a3 or c3. Nothing is done about d5 meanwhile.

1.d4 d5 2.f3.strategy: Prepares e4, but takes f3 from the g1 knight and opens the e1–h4 diagonal to the king. Black can strike at d4 at once with 2...c5, and if White pushes e4 Black can simply take the pawn.

1.d4 d5 2.h3.strategy: Stops ...Bg4, but spends a tempo on a rook-pawn move that develops nothing and leaves d5 unchallenged. Black develops freely.

1.d4 d5 2.h4.strategy: Advances a rook pawn that neither develops a piece nor challenges d5, and loosens the kingside. Black develops freely.

1.d4 d5 2.Na3.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes b5 and c4 but does little for the centre. After ...e6 the knight can be exchanged by ...Bxa3 bxa3, which leaves White with doubled a-pawns.

1.d4 d5 2.Nd2.strategy: Develops the knight and supports a later e4 or c4, but shuts in the c1 bishop until the knight moves on or b3 is played. Nothing is done against d5, so Black develops easily.

1.d4 d5 2.Nh3.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where ...Bxh3 gxh3 gives White doubled h-pawns and a weakened kingside for only the bishop pair. Even without the exchange the knight does little for the centre.

1.d4 d5 2.Bd2.strategy: Develops the bishop to a passive square where it takes d2 from the b1 knight, blocks the queen, and does nothing about d5. Black takes the lead in development.

1.d4 d5 2.Be3.strategy: Puts the bishop on the e-pawn's natural square, so e3 is no longer available, and the bishop does nothing about d5. Black develops freely.

1.d4 d5 2.Qd2.strategy: Brings the queen out early to a square where it blocks the c1 bishop and takes d2 from the b1 knight, and does nothing about d5. Black develops freely.

1.d4 d5 2.Qd3.name: Amazon Attack
1.d4 d5 2.Qd3.strategy: Brings the queen out before the minor pieces, but ...Bf5 attacks it at once, so White must spend a tempo to move it again. Black gains time and is ahead in development.

1.d4 d5 2.g4.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Zurich Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.g4.strategy: Hangs the pawn: 2...Bxg4 wins it, because the queen cannot recapture while the e2-pawn blocks the diagonal, and the kingside is weakened for nothing in return.

1.d4 d5 2.Bh6.strategy: Loses the bishop for nothing, since 2...gxh6 captures it and no White piece defends h6.

1.d4 d5 2.Kd2.strategy: Gives up castling and puts the king on a square where it blocks the c1 bishop and the queen. Black can chase it at once with developing moves.

1.d4 d5.name: Closed Game
1.d4 d5.background: 1.d4 d5 became widely popular by the early 20th century, as players with White began to try first moves other than 1.e4 more often. 1...d5 remains the second most popular reply to 1.d4, after 1...Nf6.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6.strategy: Supports d5 with the e-pawn and builds a solid centre that Black can hold for a long time. White keeps the tension on d5 and usually has a little more space. The cost is the c8-bishop, shut in behind e6, which needs a freeing pawn break or a fianchetto before it plays a part.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6.strategy: Defends d5 with the c-pawn and keeps the c8-bishop's diagonal open, so the bishop is not buried behind the pawn chain. If Black later takes on c4, the c6-pawn supports ...b5 to hold the pawn or to gain time against the capturing piece. The drawbacks are that c6 develops no piece and takes that square from the b8-knight, and that the freeing break ...c5 costs a tempo.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4.strategy: Takes the pawn and gives up the centre in return for free piece play. Black usually lets White regain the pawn and spends the time striking at White's centre, because holding the pawn tends to be unprofitable. White's aim is to use the extra space in the centre to build an attack.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nc6.strategy: Develops with quick pressure on d4, but the knight blocks the c-pawn and Black no longer holds d5 with a pawn. Black gets active pieces in return and must be willing to trade a bishop for a knight. It is playable and a useful surprise, but its theory is less developed than that of the main defences.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5.strategy: Develops the bishop before ...e6 can shut it in, but leaves b7 undefended, so 3.Qb3 hits it at once, and after an exchange on d5 White gains time against Black's queen and bishop. It is an offbeat but playable way to solve the problem of the c8-bishop.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5.strategy: Sacrifices a pawn for a wedge on d4 and some attacking chances, developing quickly and often castling queenside. White usually returns the pawn at a good moment to gain a positional edge. The pawn on d4 is stronger than it looks, so careless play by White is punished.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c5.strategy: Mirrors White's move and challenges d4 at once. After cxd5 Black should not retake with the queen, since White then develops with a gain of time. Theory holds that White keeps an edge and that Black plays at best for a draw.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight but leaves d5 to the queen: 3.cxd5 Nxd5 4.e4 drives the knight away with a gain of time and gives White a broad pawn centre. Supporting d5 first with a pawn avoids this.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Na6.strategy: Aims at b4 from the rim but does nothing in the centre and leaves d5 to the queen alone. After 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 the queen is driven back, and White leads in development.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Be6.strategy: Guards d5 a second time, but the bishop blocks the e-pawn and leaves b7 undefended. After 3.cxd5 Bxd5 4.Nc3 it comes under attack again, and White develops with a gain of time.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bg4.strategy: Gets the bishop out early, but on g4 it hits only the well-defended e2-pawn and leaves b7 undefended. 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 gains time against the queen, and a pawn move later chases the bishop.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Qd7.strategy: Keeps d5 guarded but puts the queen on d7, where it blocks the c8-bishop and takes d7 from the b8-knight. After 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 the queen has to move again, and White is ahead in development.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Qd6.strategy: Brings the queen out early to hold d5, but after 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 it must move again while White develops with tempo.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nh6.strategy: Heads for f5 from the rim, but the c1-bishop already eyes h6: 3.Bxh6 gxh6 wrecks Black's kingside pawns, with only the bishop pair in return. The d5 pawn is also left to the queen.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5 for the case of ...dxc4, but spends a tempo on a rook-pawn move and leaves d5 to the queen. After 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 the queen is attacked and must retreat.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 a5.strategy: A wing move that weakens b5 and contributes nothing to the centre or development. White plays 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 and gains a tempo against the queen.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, but there the bishop would face its own d5-pawn, and d5 is left to the queen alone. 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 drives the queen off with a gain of time.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 f6.strategy: Takes f6 from the knight and weakens e6 and the e8-h5 diagonal, while neither supporting d5 nor developing a piece. White answers 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 and gains a tempo.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 f5.strategy: Stakes out e4 with a kingside pawn, but leaves d5 to the queen and weakens e6 and the e8-h5 diagonal. 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 gains time against the queen.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 g6.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto ...Bg7 but ignores the centre. 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 chases the queen away, and White keeps the bigger centre and the lead in development.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 h6.strategy: Takes g5 from the c1-bishop, but it is a slow rim-pawn move that does nothing for d5 or development. After 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 White hits the queen with tempo.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 h5.strategy: Spends a tempo on the rim and loosens g5 and g6, with no connection to d5 or to development. White answers 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 and develops with a gain of time.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nd7.strategy: Blocks the queen's defence of d5, so 3.cxd5 wins a pawn: after 3...Ngf6 4.Nc3 and e4 White keeps it. The knight on d7 also shuts in the c8-bishop.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bd7.strategy: Blocks the queen's defence of d5, so 3.cxd5 wins a pawn that no black piece can retake at once. The bishop on d7 is passive and takes d7 from the b8-knight.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bh3.strategy: Gives away the bishop for nothing: 3.gxh3 takes it, and no black piece can recapture on h3, so Black has no compensation at all.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Kd7.strategy: Gives up castling and blocks the queen's defence of d5, so 3.cxd5 wins a pawn that cannot be retaken at once. The king is left in the middle with nothing in return.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 b5.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Zilbermints Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.c4 b5.strategy: Offers the b-pawn to deflect the c-pawn, but 3.cxb5 wins it, since nothing can recapture, and Black has no lead in development to show for it. The queenside is loosened for good.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 g5.strategy: Leaves the g-pawn en prise: 3.Bxg5 takes it along the open c1-h6 diagonal, and nothing of Black's can retake, since the queen's diagonal is blocked by e7. The kingside is loosened for good with no development in return.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square and controls e4, while committing the c- and e-pawns to nothing yet. That flexibility is the strength and the cost: White still decides what kind of game it becomes, from a Queen's Gambit to quiet set-ups with an early bishop move.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c6.strategy: Supports d5 with a pawn and keeps the c8-bishop's route to f5 or g4 open, since ...e6 has not been played. It is solid and differs little from 2...Nf6 in most lines. The cost is that the b8-knight loses its natural c6-square.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 e6.strategy: Supports d5 and opens the f8-bishop's diagonal, a solid set-up that differs little from 2...Nf6 in most lines. The cost is the c8-bishop, now shut in behind the e6-pawn, which usually has to wait for a fianchetto or a later central pawn break to find a diagonal.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nc6.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Chigorin Variation
1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nc6.background: This is the knight move of the Chigorin Defence, 1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nc6, named after the 19th-century Russian master Mikhail Chigorin and considered playable but rare. After 3.c4 this position transposes into that defence's 3.Nf3 line.
1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece at once and pressures d4, but the knight blocks the c-pawn, so d5 can no longer be supported by ...c6. With only the queen guarding d5, White can hit it immediately with c4.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Bf5.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6 closes it in, a mirror image of White's own bishop-first set-up. The cost is that the b7-pawn loses its only defender, and 3.Nh4 attacks the bishop at once, aiming to trade the knight for it.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Bg4.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Anti-Torre
1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Bg4.strategy: Develops the bishop actively and prepares ...Bxf3, which would double White's f-pawns. But 3.Ne5 attacks the bishop and gains a tempo, and with the bishop gone from c8 the b7-pawn has no defender.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 at once and brings tension into the centre instead of defending d5 passively. The cost is time and structure: if White takes on c5, Black must spend moves regaining the pawn, and d5 has little support meanwhile. It aims for an active game rather than a solid one.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop before the centre is settled. It is sound, but without …Nf6 or …c6 the d5-pawn has only the queen to guard it, so 3.c4 puts pressure on it at once.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nd7.strategy: Blocks the c8-bishop, and the knight does little on d7 before a pawn move supports d5. White can develop or take space undisturbed.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes b4 and c5 but is far from the centre. It costs a tempo for little, and White can simply carry on building.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Bd7.strategy: Puts the bishop on a passive square, where it blocks the queen and takes d7 from the b8-knight. White can continue with a free hand.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Be6.strategy: Shuts in the e-pawn, so …e6 is no longer possible. The bishop guards d5, but it invites 3.Ng5, which attacks it and threatens Nxe6 fxe6 to double Black's pawns.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Qd7.strategy: Brings the queen out early and blocks the c8-bishop. 3.Ne5 attacks it at once and gains a tempo, with the d4-pawn guarding the knight.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Qd6.strategy: Brings the queen out early to an exposed square. 3.Nc3 threatens Nb5, which would attack both the queen and c7.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nh6.strategy: Aims for f5 but invites 3.Bxh6 gxh6, which wrecks Black's kingside pawns into doubled, isolated h-pawns. The bishop pair is little compensation.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 a6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a flank move that has no role yet. At best it prepares ...b5, while White is free to continue developing.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 a5.strategy: A rim pawn move that only controls b4 and leaves b5 without pawn cover. It develops nothing, and White builds up freely.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, but that bishop would only look at Black's own d5-pawn, and c6 is weakened. White can develop freely.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 b5.strategy: Stops c4 for now but leaves the pawn loose: 3.e3 already threatens Bxb5+. It develops nothing and leaves c6 without pawn cover.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 f6.strategy: Prepares ...e5 but takes f6 from the g8-knight and weakens e6 and the e8–h5 diagonal. White develops freely while Black's development lags behind.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 f5.strategy: Plays for a Dutch-style set-up, but the pawn weakens e6 and the king's diagonal and leaves e5 as an outpost for White's knight. Black must still develop all the pieces behind it.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 h6.strategy: A slow move that takes g5 from White's pieces but develops nothing. White uses the tempo to develop.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 h5.strategy: Gains space on the flank at the cost of a tempo and the g5-square: the h-pawn can no longer drive a White piece from g5, and the advanced pawn can become a target.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Bh3.strategy: Hangs the bishop: 3.gxh3 wins a whole piece for nothing, since the bishop on h3 is attacked by the g2-pawn and defended by nothing.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Kd7.strategy: Gives up castling for nothing and walks into 3.Ne5+, which forces the king to move again. Black loses more time, and the king stays stuck in the centre.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 e5.strategy: Offers a pawn for no clear return: after 3.dxe5 the pawn is gone, and ...d4 would lose a second one to Nxd4. Black has little to show against a White position without weaknesses.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 g5.strategy: Hangs a pawn at once: 3.Bxg5 or 3.Nxg5 wins it, and the loosened kingside offers no compensation.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and guards d5 and e4, so Black commits to no pawn structure yet. The knight keeps both a solid set-up and a sharp counter against the undefended b2-pawn available.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 at once and aims to profit from the bishop having left c1: ...Qb6 will press on the undefended b2-pawn before Black has castled. Black offers the c-pawn for quick development and activity, so White usually declines it and keeps two pawns in the centre. The game is sharp, with counterplay for Black.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 e6.strategy: Supports d5 in the manner of the Queen's Gambit Declined and opens the f8-bishop's path to d6, where it can challenge White's bishop. The cost is the c8-bishop, which the e6-pawn shuts in and which often struggles to find a good square. The game is solid and strategic.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 c6.strategy: Supports d5 in Slav style and keeps the c8-bishop free to come out to f5, while the queen gains b6 against the undefended b2-pawn. The c6-pawn takes that square from the b8-knight, but the set-up is solid and leads to a calm, strategic game.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Bf5.background: The Göttingen manuscript, the earliest known work devoted entirely to modern chess, already includes 1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Bf5 among its twelve openings; the possible dates given for it are 1500–1505 and 1471. Jacob Sarratt's “A Treatise on the Game of Chess” (1808) gives the line as well, continuing 3.Nc3 Nc6 4.f3.
1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Bf5.strategy: Mirrors White's development and brings the bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6 can shut it in. The symmetrical structure is sound but offers Black few winning chances, and without a transposition the game tends toward a quiet draw. White's most testing plan is to steer into a Queen's Gambit with c4.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Nc6.strategy: Develops the knight with pressure on d4 and prepares to bring out the c8-bishop actively and to strike later with ...e5. It blocks the c-pawn, so it can no longer support the centre, and d4 is easy for White to keep guarded.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Nd7.strategy: Develops the knight to a square from which it supports ...e5 and ...c5 and leaves the c-pawn free to support the centre. It blocks the c8-bishop and the queen's file, so Black is slightly cramped, and White can build the usual London set-up undisturbed.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Bg4.strategy: Pins the e2-pawn against the queen, so 3.e3 is ruled out for now: 3...Bxd1 would follow. White can simply develop, or question the bishop at once.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, but with the pawn already on d5 the bishop bites on its own pawn for the time being. The move develops nothing yet and loosens c6, so White can build the usual London set-up at leisure.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the kingside bishop, which then presses on d4 along the long diagonal. It is sound but slow, and White meets it with the usual London set-up.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 h5.strategy: An uncommon sideline with a trap: the routine 3.e3? closes the bishop's retreat to d2, and 3...e5! lets Black trap it with ...f6, ...g5 and ...h4 and win it for pawns. White avoids this by keeping the retreat open, for example with a developing knight move, after which the h-pawn does little for Black.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it aims at b4 and c5 but takes little part in the fight for the centre. It does guard c7, yet costs time that White uses to build the usual London set-up.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Bd7.strategy: Puts the bishop on a passive square, where it takes d7 from the b8-knight and blocks the queen's d-file. It does less than ...Bf5 would, and White simply goes on developing.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Be6.strategy: Puts the bishop on e6, where it blocks the e-pawn and with it the f8-bishop, so the usual plan of freeing that bishop is gone. White develops at leisure while the bishop does little.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Qd7.strategy: Brings the queen out early, where it blocks the c8-bishop and the knight and can be hit with tempo by a White knight. Black spends time on the queen instead of developing.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Nh6.strategy: Heads for f5 or g4 but offers the trade 3.Bxh6 gxh6, after which the doubled, isolated h-pawns are a lasting weakness in Black's kingside.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 a6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a flank move that only prepares ...b5. It develops no piece and leaves the centre alone, so White develops unhindered.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 a5.strategy: Spends a tempo on a rook-pawn advance that takes b4 but develops nothing and does not contest the centre. White develops and gains space at leisure.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 b5.strategy: Pushes the b-pawn without developing a piece, weakens c5 and c6 and makes the pawn a target: after 3.e3 the f1-bishop threatens Bxb5+, and a4 can attack it too. Black then spends further moves to hold it.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 f6.strategy: Aims for ...e5 but takes f6 from the g8-knight and opens the e8–h5 diagonal, so once White has played e3 the queen can check on h5. Black spends a tempo without developing a piece, while White simply develops.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 f5.strategy: Aims for a solid wall of pawns on f5, e6 and d5, but weakens e6 and the e8–h5 diagonal and leaves e5 as a permanent hole, which the f4-bishop already controls and a knight can occupy from f3. Once the wall stands, the c8-bishop is hemmed in behind its own pawns.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 h6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a rook-pawn move that develops nothing; its point, a later ...g5 against the f4-bishop, would loosen Black's own kingside. White simply develops, and h3 gives the bishop a retreat on h2.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Bh3.strategy: Gives up the bishop for nothing: 3.Nxh3 or 3.gxh3 wins it, and Black has no compensation for the piece.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Qd6.strategy: Puts the queen where the f4-bishop takes it: 3.Bxd6 wins the queen, and after the recapture Black has only a bishop in return.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 Kd7.strategy: Gives up castling for good and puts the king in front of the queen and the c8-bishop, blocking both. After 3.e3 the f1-bishop can already check on b5, and the king stays exposed in the centre.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 e5.strategy: Offers a pawn that 3.Bxe5 simply wins: the bishop can retreat when attacked, d4 stays guarded by the queen, and Black has opened the position but has no compensation for the pawn.

1.d4 d5 2.Bf4 g5.strategy: Hangs the g-pawn: 3.Bxg5 wins it, because the queen cannot recapture with the e7-pawn in the way, and the bishop remains active. The advance also weakens the kingside for nothing.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the kingside knight, adds a second guard to d5 and watches e4, so White cannot easily build a pawn centre. Black keeps the pawn structure open for now and gets a sound, flexible game; White decides how sharp it gets, from quiet development to a gambit for the initiative.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 c6.strategy: Supports d5 with a pawn, takes b5 from the knight and leaves the c8-bishop's diagonal open, so the bishop can come out before ...e6. It aims at a solid pawn structure. The cost is that the b8-knight loses c6 and usually goes to d7.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 e6.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Chigorin Variation
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 e6.strategy: Supports d5 and opens the f8-bishop, heading for French Defence structures, which 3.e4 transposes to. The price is the usual one in the French: the c8-bishop is shut in behind the e6-pawn. Black gets a solid, fairly closed game.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Develops with pressure on d4, but the knight blocks the c-pawn, so ...c6 can no longer support d5. Sound but offbeat.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Bf5.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Chigorin Variation, Alburt Defence
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Bf5.strategy: Develops the light-squared bishop before ...e6 can shut it in. It becomes a target, though: White gains kingside space and time by harassing it with pawns. Sound but rarely played.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Bg4.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Chigorin Variation, Anti-Veresov
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Bg4.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6 shuts it in, with ...Bxf3 available once the knight comes to f3. The bishop is easy to harass, so White gains time and kingside space with pawn moves against it. Playable, but Black spends time on the bishop.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 c5.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Chigorin Variation, Irish Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 at once and offers the c-pawn. Taking it with the d-pawn gives up the centre, and Black aims to win the pawn back with a quick bishop; developing the c1-bishop and recapturing on d4 instead declines with a slight edge for White. Viable, but a rare and little-explored sideline.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 e5.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Chigorin Variation, Shaviliuk Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 e5.strategy: Offers the e-pawn to gain space with ...d4: after 3.dxe5 d4 the knight must move, and on 4.Ne4 the reply 4...Qd5 attacks the knight and e5 together and wins the pawn back. The gambit is rare, and its value is unclear.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 f5.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Veresov Attack, Dutch System
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 f5.strategy: Sets up a Stonewall structure, with the pawns on d5 and f5 holding e4. The price is a weak e5-square and an open e8-h5 diagonal, and 3.e4 fxe4 4.Qh5+ g6 5.Qxd5 wins the pawn back at once. Playable but rare and risky.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes b4 and c5 but does nothing for d5 or e4. White takes the centre and leads in development.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Be6.strategy: Stands in front of the e-pawn, so neither ...e6 nor ...e5 can follow, and the f8-bishop can only come out by way of ...g6. White has the freer centre and more space.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Qd7.strategy: Blocks the c8-bishop and takes d7 from the b8-knight, a queen move that develops nothing and does nothing for the centre. White develops with the better centre.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Qd6.strategy: Brings the queen out early, where it is a target: 3.Nb5 hits it and c7, and 3.e4 dxe4 4.Nxe4 attacks it with tempo, leaving White ahead in development.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nh6.strategy: Allows 3.Bxh6 gxh6, which doubles Black's h-pawns and breaks up the kingside, with only the bishop pair in return.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 a6.strategy: Takes b5 from the knight but spends a tempo on a rim pawn without developing anything. White takes the centre and leads in development.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 a5.strategy: Spends a tempo on a rim pawn and gives up control of b6, without helping the centre or developing a piece. White takes the centre with 3.e4.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 b6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the c8-bishop but does nothing for d5, so White takes the centre with 3.e4 and gets more space and easier development.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 f6.strategy: Prepares ...e5, but takes f6 from the g8-knight and opens the e8-h5 diagonal to the black king. White takes the centre with quicker development.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the f8-bishop but does nothing for d5, so White takes the centre with 3.e4 and develops faster.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 h6.strategy: Takes g5 from the c1-bishop but spends a tempo on a rim pawn, so White takes the centre with 3.e4 and develops faster.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 h5.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Chigorin Variation, Shropshire Defence
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 h5.strategy: Spends a tempo on a rim pawn that develops nothing and does nothing for the centre, and it gives up control of g6. White simply develops.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Nd7.strategy: Blocks the queen's defence of d5 as well as the c8-bishop, and nothing else guards the pawn, so 3.Nxd5 wins it.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Bd7.strategy: Blocks the queen's defence of d5, which has no other guard, so 3.Nxd5 wins a pawn. The bishop also takes d7 from the b8-knight.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Bh3.strategy: Hangs the bishop to 3.gxh3, with no compensation at all.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 Kd7.strategy: Gives up castling and blocks the queen's defence of d5, so 3.Nxd5 wins a pawn, and the king on d7 also shuts in the c8-bishop.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 b5.strategy: Drops a pawn to 3.Nxb5. Black has nothing to regain it with: 3...Ba6 is met by 4.Nc3, and White keeps the extra pawn.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 g5.strategy: Drops a pawn to 3.Bxg5 and weakens the whole kingside for nothing.

1.d4 d5 2.Bg5 Bg4.strategy: Answers the bishop with the same move: each bishop now looks at the other side's e-pawn with the queen behind it. The symmetry is shallow, since White moves first and decides when and how it is broken, so Black gains nothing from copying.
1.d4 d5 2.Bg5 Bg4.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Levitsky Attack, Welling Variation

1.d4 d5 2.e3 Nf6.name: Queen's Pawn Game
1.d4 d5 2.e3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square, where it controls e4. White's e3 has shut in the bishop on c1 for the moment, so Black can simply develop and see what set-up White chooses, with a solid pawn on d5 and nothing to fear.

1.d4 d5 2.h4 c5.strategy: Hits d4 at once and takes space on the queenside. White's h-pawn move has done nothing for the centre or for development, so Black can strike at the centre first and the d4 pawn has to be defended.

1.d4 d5 2.e3 Nf6 3.Bd3.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Stonewall Attack
1.d4 d5 2.e3 Nf6 3.Bd3.background: The Stonewall Attack became established in master play after Harry Nelson Pillsbury won all six games in which he used it at the two New York tournaments of 1893. It began to disappear from top-level chess by the early 1920s but remains a popular choice at club level.
1.d4 d5 2.e3 Nf6 3.Bd3.strategy: Develops the bishop to its most active diagonal, aiming at h7, and builds a compact pawn chain, with a later f4 to control e5 and prepare a kingside attack. The price is an inflexible structure, weak light squares and a c1-bishop shut in behind its own pawns.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 e6 3.Bf4.name: Rapport-Jobava System, with e6
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 e6 3.Bf4.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before e3 can shut it in, eyeing c7 and e5. White pairs it with the knight on c3 to build an active set-up, while Black, with e6 played, has a solid but slightly passive light-squared bishop.

1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 f5 3.e4.name: Dutch Defence: Kingfisher Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.Nc3 f5 3.e4.strategy: A pawn gambit: the e-pawn is offered at once to open the centre and exploit the loosened kingside and a lead in development. Black can simply accept the pawn and develop, and White has to prove its compensation.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Bf5 3.c4.strategy: Challenges d5 at once, which is now attacked by the pawn and defended only by the queen. Black's early bishop move has not added a defender to d5, so Black must decide at once how to hold the centre.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Bf5 3.c4 e6.strategy: Defends d5 with a pawn and opens the f8-bishop. The c8-bishop is already outside the chain, so the usual worry about it being shut in by this move does not arise, and Black gets a solid centre.

1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Bf5 3.c4 e6 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops the queenside knight and adds a second attacker to d5, so the pressure on Black's centre is now real. White has a sound set-up against the d-pawn, while Black's bishop is already outside the chain, so the fight is over whether d5 can be held.
